Helm is often called "the package manager for Kubernetes." Just as apt or brew helps you
install and manage idx_cf6cc0a6 software on your operating system, Helm helps you install and manage
applications on your Kubernetes cluster.
To understand how Helm accomplishes this, we need to explore its fundamental building
blocks.
Traffic flow: NodePort → Service → Pod
When you open the URL that minikube gives you, here is the path your request takes:
Browser → NodePort on the minikube node → flask-app-service (stable DNS + load
balancer) → one of the healthy Pods matching label app: flask-app
The Service is the stable layer in the middle. Pods can come and go, but the Service's
address never changes, so clients are always decoupled from the individual Pod
instances behind it.

The three core elements of the Docker CNM are as follows:
Sandbox: A network namespace for a container where its network stack resides
Endpoint: An interface that connects a container to a network
Network: A collection of endpoints that can communicate with each other directly
To create a custom Docker bridge network called frontend, you can use the docker network create
command with the --driver flag set to bridge (which is the default driver) and the --subnet flag to
specify the subnet for the network. Here's an example command:
$ docker network create --driver bridge \
--subnet 172.25.0.0/16 frontend
This will create a bridge network named frontend with a subnet of 172.25.0.0/16. You can then use this
network when starting containers with the --network option:
$ docker container run --network frontend <docker-image>
To run two nginx:alpine containers attached to the frontend network that we created earlier, you can
use the following docker container run commands:
$ docker container run --name nginx1 --network frontend -d \
nginx:alpine
$ docker container run --name nginx2 --network frontend -d \
nginx:alpine
These commands will start two containers named nginx1 and nginx2 with the nginx:alpine image and
attach them to the frontend network. The -d flag runs the containers in the background as daemons. You
can then access the containers by their container names (nginx1 and nginx2) or their IP addresses within
the frontend network.

199 The Observability Agent: Real-Life Use Cases
Reason phase
The agent can take idx_87511419 the information from the perceive phase into the reason phase and idx_29eaed53 craft a
human-readable response or an execution plan for further actions. Some observability
platforms, Dynatrace being one example, also provide their own built-in reasoning, which can
directly provide an explanation of the perceived data, including a remediation action plan. We
have seen an example in Chapter 3 in the AIOps: reducing the noise with anomaly and root cause
detection section. There, the built-in LLM provides textual output including an explanation of
the data, root cause, and remediation steps. An agentic AI can use this output directly from the
observability tool during the reason phase, without having to rely on its own LLMs and RAG to
plan actions.
Act phase
The act phase idx_3328c3e3 would idx_e78e60b5 typically involve interaction with external tools that can make code or
configuration changes, such as proposing a code fix for the identified vulnerability or
proposing a change in the Kubernetes deployment manifests to adapt scaling or workload
sizing settings.
There are, however, use cases where agentic AI reaches out to the observability platform to
make changes there. Here are three examples:
Set up SLO-based alerting for the top three API endpoints of my service
Mark the detected problem as "in progress" or "known issue" and mute alerting for
now
Validate my release based on all observability signals you have, and give me a thumbs
up or down
The last example is common for those observability platforms that provide built-in
automation workflows to automate tasks such as automated validation of a release, a feature
flag, or even orchestrating remediation for problems. Dynatrace, New Relic, Datadog, and
probably other platforms provide similar built-in capabilities. If you have created workflows in
your observability platform that automate certain tasks, it's best for the agentic AI to simply
reuse those by triggering them, rather than replicating the individual steps.
Learn phase
Once an idx_0556fc0e action is idx_ee69cadc executed, it's time to learn whether that action had the intended effect. The
learn phase typically includes the agentic AI asking the user whether the proposed actions
solved the initial problem statement. That's valuable feedback that the agent can use the next
time a similar request comes up.
